summary: For ages 9–11, teach that we see a non-luminous object because light travels from a source to the object, reflects off it, and then enters the eye (source → object → eye, one way only). Light sources such as lamps are seen by light travelling directly from them into the eye. The central obstacle is the intuitive extramission belief that something leaves the eye to 'reach out' and see. Surface this belief first with diagnostic drawing/probes, then teach refutationally — name and reject the wrong idea and build the full arrowed ray path — and connect to diffuse reflection so dull everyday objects count as light senders. Because gains often revert, revisit and re-test over time.
misconceptions: Extramission: the eye sends something out (rays/'visual feelers') to see the object.
Light travels both ways — into the eye from luminous things but out of the eye toward non-luminous things.
Seeing just requires light to 'land on' and brighten the object; the reflected-into-the-eye step is missing.
A whole image or picture of the object flies intact into the eye.
Once eyes 'adjust', we can see in complete darkness.
Only shiny surfaces reflect light into the eye, so dull objects are seen by some other means.

activities.title: Make yourself able to see it: route the light path
steps: In an on-screen model of a dark scene with a hidden object (e.g. a mug on a table), take on the goal: 'make yourself able to see it.' (In this model the rays you draw control what can be seen; in real life, drawing arrows does not change what you see.)
First try your own intuition: draw an arrow pointing FROM the eye toward the mug, and notice what happens.
Place a movable lamp and draw a light ray from the lamp to the mug; check whether that alone is enough.
Complete the full chain: lamp → mug → reflected arrow → eye, with a direction arrow on every ray.
Toggle the lamp off and describe what happens to the mug and why.
Swap the shiny mug for a dull matt object and check whether it can still be seen; explain why.
activities.insight: Seeing is not the eye reaching out; it is light arriving AT the eye after bouncing off the object. If no light reaches the object or no reflected light reaches the eye, the object cannot be seen. Shiny surfaces reflect light mostly in one direction, like a mirror, and dull surfaces scatter it in many directions, so both can send light to the eye.

activities.title: Elicit and refute: 'How do you think you can see this book?'
steps: Before any teaching, draw or describe how you see a nearby object such as a book ('draw how you see this book').
Answer a Socratic optician/vision-scientist persona who asks what you think travels, and in which direction, when you look at the book.
When prompted, decide whether anything leaves your eye, and justify your answer.
Re-draw the path after the discussion, adding a direction arrow to every ray.
activities.insight: Putting your own theory into words exposes the hidden extramission assumption so it can be named and replaced with the one-way source→object→eye path.

activities.title: Physical receiver model: the eye is something light ENTERS
steps: Use string or wool to physically trace the light path from the lamp to the object and then to the eye position.
Observe a camera obscura or a webcam used as a model 'eye', noticing that an image forms only because light enters it.
Line up three holes in cards (or a tube) so light reaches the eye only along a straight path, and check what happens when one card is shifted out of line.
State in your own words which way the light must be travelling for the image to form.
activities.insight: Because an image only forms when light goes INTO the model eye (camera/webcam/obscura), the eye must be a receiver of light, not a sender; light also travels in straight lines along the traced path.

activities.title: Predict–observe–explain: block the line of sight
steps: Look at a brightly lit toy or apple you can clearly see.
Predict: if a card is slid between the object and your eye while the object stays fully lit, will you still see it? Say why before testing.
Slide the card and observe the result.

Explain what this shows: the space between the object and your eye must be clear. Then, using the lamp-off and dark-room evidence as well, explain why scientists say the light travels from the object into your eye.
Answer follow-up probes: does the light still reach the object if you close your eyes? Could you ever see it by waiting in a truly pitch-black room? How is your eye like a camera?
activities.insight: The object is still fully lit, yet blocking the space between object and eye stops you seeing it, so the path from object to eye must be clear. Put together with the fact that you cannot see anything without a light source (even with your eyes open), this supports the model that light travels FROM the object INTO the eye, and seeing does not 'make' the light.

activities.title: Delayed re-check: sequence, draw, and refute
steps: Sequence the three steps of the journey into the correct order: source → object → eye.
Answer a refutational check such as 'Does anything leave your eye when you see something?' and justify your choice.
Draw the complete ray path for a new everyday object, with a direction arrow on every ray.
Revisit this check days or weeks later to confirm the idea has held.
activities.insight: Being able to re-sequence, reject the outgoing-eye arrow, and draw the full path on a delayed test shows the model has genuinely replaced the intuition rather than been temporarily memorised.

checkQuestion: A girl is looking at an apple sitting on a table in a well-lit room. Explain what has to happen with the light for her to see the apple — trace the light's journey from start to finish.
checkAnswer: Light travels from a source (the lamp or sun) to the apple, reflects (bounces) off the apple, and then travels into her eye. Her eye receives the light — nothing comes out of her eye.
